Children’s Fancy Dress Party The children of the Waimata Valley had a joyous time on Saturday afternoon, when the Waimata Valley Womens’ Institute celebrated its fifth birthday with a children’s fancy dress party in the local hall. Gaily decorated with coloured streamers and its walls hung with gift parcels, the hall looked most attractive. To each gift was attached a playing card, and on arrival each child was given a card and told to find ,ts equivalent on the wall and to take the gift accompanying it. This provided a popular competition, which was entered into with zest by the young guests. Jolly games, organised by Mesdames Shanks and J. C. Mazengarb, were played in the grounds, and later a delicious party tea, including rainbow-hued fruit jellies, home-made sweets, orange drinks and other tasty fare, was served at tables on the wide verandah. The children were seated at the tables, which were furnished with bon-bons, squeakers, masks and other ’favours. Coloured balloons adorned the verandah.

Handsome Birthday Cake A handsome birthday cake, made and iced by one of the institute members, was carried out in the institute colours, yellow and blue, and surmounted by five lighted candles. The cake was cut by Mrs. F. E. Rogers, who had resided in the valley, longer than anyone else present, and the candle-lights were blown out by little Doreen Gambirazzi, who was dressed in yellow and blue to represent the institute.

The majority of the children wore fancy costumes, which gave a festive appearance to the hall and grounds, the prevailing choice being cowboy garb for the boys and Dutch national dress for the girls. The costumes were judged by Mesdames P. Quinn, F. E. Rogers, and R. C. Aires, the awards being made .n sections according to age, a boy and girl in each group receiving a prize as follow; —Four years and under.— Kitty Graham (Egyptian) and Jonathan Graham (Cowboy), these tiny tots not being related although having the same surname. From five to nine years—Mary Baillie (Egyptian) and Brian Newman (Gnome). Over nine.

Eve Graham (Dutch Girl) and Jim Robinson (Pillar Box). A special prize was donated to Doreen Gambirazzi for her representation of the institute.

Items by the Children

During the afternoon several enjoyable items were given by some of the school' children present, including a playette, “A Monkey and Two Cats,” by Janet Newman, Mary Proudfoot, and Cecil Gillgren; a recitation by infant pupils; and a recitation, ‘‘Bad Sir Brian Bottomley," by Sammy and Clarrie Gillgren and Peter Scott. The guests were welcomed by the president of the institute, Mrs. J. L. Graham, and the entertainment was organised and managed by institute members.

The adults present were served with a ‘buffet tea when the children had finished their repast. Death of Joseph Paton
* Joseph was born 14 Feb 1813 in Dundee, Scotland, a (possible) twin with John Paton. He was a Labourer and assisted in surveying Motueka. He was working at Thoms Sawmill at the time of his death aged 31
Nelson Examiner, 25 May 1844
FATAL ACCIDENT A man named Paton, employed at Thoms' Sawmill, Motueka, met with an accident last week which cost him his life. Whilst engaged in grinding tools at a stone attached to the machinery his clothes were caught in the saws and he was drawn up and cut about the head in a most frightful manner. After lingering five days he died leaving a wife and four children.
* Amelia was born, in Auckland, 4 years after Joseph's death. Her father has been rumoured to have been Joseph's twin brother John. He was still living in Motueka at this time but Margaret would no doubt have left town and moved North. She is not registered at BDM as Paton. Margaret, did remarry but not until 25 April 1853, to William Douglas (1805-1867). Wilhemina married as Paton in 1864, so she would have been brought up with that name.

@I103@.name: William Satterthwaite
notes:
About William Satterthwaite

William, son of Clement bapt 20 Jan 1623/24 William, son of Clement bapt 20 Mar 1630/31 William, son of Clement bapt 23 Nov 1634 William, son of Clement bur 5 Nov 1635 William, son of Clement bur 6 Jul 1636 William, son of Clement *bapt 3 Mar 1648/49

Fowkes and Ridley [1988] identify the last William as the son of Clement and father of Michael, born 1676/78 when that William would have been 29 years of age. However, Ruth Satterthwaite writes that the Pickard family tree diagrams from England show William born in 1632 (but show his brother Edward born in 1630 instead of 1638, and do not show either Charles or Dorothy as children of Clement). She adds that the Satterthwaite genealogy [Satterthwaite, 1910] is silent on the date of his birth.

Fowkes and Ridley name Charles, born 11 Mar 1632/1633, as the eldest son of Clement. If that is correct, then the first William above could not be this one, nor one "born in 1632". and we are left with 23 Nov 1634 or 3 Mar 1648/49 if the Parish Register is complete in this regard. With a son Daniel born in 1689, the earlier William would at that time have been aged 65, and the other aged 40, much the more likely. I'm therefore accepting the Fowkes and Ridley birth date.

William, of Cragg, was imprisoned in 1665 and 1666 for refusal to take oaths, and again in 1684 with his brother Edward of Townend for refusing to answer upon oath in a civil trial [Satterthwaite, 1914].

In 1704, an indenture was made the eleventh day of May between Edward, his son Benjamin, both of Town End, Tanners (uncle and cousin of William), and William Satterthwaite, Elder of Beckside, all in Coulthouse, to sell for fifty shillings a tract of land at Town End in Coulthouse for use as a burial place for "the people of God called Quakers" [Satterthwaite, 1914]. The two dozen purchasers of the land included "Willm Satterthwt & John Satterthwaite of Cragg Tanners" and James Satterthwt of Greenend yeoman. Another of those was Nicholas Tyson of ffyeldhead, yeoman, whose surname is the same as that of Esther Tyson who married William's grandson William and emigrated to Bucks County.

Ruth Satterthwaite reports the burial of this William on 11 Dec 1719, and of his widow Agnes15 Feb 1722. However, records of these do not appear in the Colthouse Burial Register, so I do not know the source of the dates. I accept instead the death and burial recorded for 13 and 15 Oct 1717 of "William of Beckside in Colthouse", as being this William [Satterthwaite, 1914]. That record describes William as "An ancient Friend & writer of Friends' Records for Hawkshead", and adds that he was fined 10/- for attending the meeting at George Braithwaite's and £5 in lieu of the unknown preacher at that meeting. Death: [Satterthwaite, 1914]

Agnes' father William was of High Wray [Satterthwaite, 1914]. We don't know what William Braithwaite's relationship was to George Braithwaite of High Wray, whose daughter Dorothy married William's brother Edward.

The six children of William and Agnes (Braithwaite) Satterthwaite: John, Michael, William, Rebecca, Hester and Daniel.
